title: Chatbot Workshop
tagline: You write a program that asks a question, waits for the answer, and uses what was typed.
objectives: Write a line that asks a question and keeps the answer in a variable.
Use what somebody typed in what my program says back to them.
Read what Python says when it stops, and work out which line to change.

config.headline: Today your program talks back.
lines: Every program you have run in here does exactly the same thing every time you press RUN. Today's does not. Today you build a chatbot.
A chatbot is a program that asks the person at the keyboard a question, waits for them to type an answer, and then uses what they typed in what it says next.

It is not clever and it is not alive. It follows a list of instructions somebody typed, in the same order, every single time. That list does three jobs over and over: ask a question, keep the answer in a variable, then print a reply that uses what is in the variable.
You met variables last lesson. A variable is a name with an = after it, and whatever you put on the right of the = is kept in it. Today the thing you keep is whatever the person typed.
One thing worth knowing before you start. Whatever somebody types is kept as WORDS, every single time, even if they type a number. That is why you can join it straight onto a sentence with a +.
Here is a small one running. Watch it once before you build your own.
Here is the hour, in order.
First a short film with no sound, then three training builds where the bot gets less and less finished for you.
Then twelve minutes on your own bot, with two questions you pick yourself.
Then the Chatbot Swap. Somebody else in this room, at another computer, gets your bot and tries to break it, and you get theirs. You will each write the other a short report about it.
You are not told who your partner is until the very end. You each get a call sign instead — a made-up name, like Spanner 7 — and that is the name on their screen and yours.
It finishes with one marked question and a screen that asks you how the hour went.

config.title: A bot that says hello
config.intro:
Every chatbot on the planet is built out of the same three jobs, one after the other: ask, keep, reply. This first bot does each of them exactly once, so you can see all three at the same time.

The bot on this card is not finished. There is a real mistake in it, put there on purpose. You will press RUN, Python will tell you what is wrong, and you will put it right.

config.title: Somebody else is about to use your bot
config.intro:
Every program in the world gets used by somebody who did not write it, and that is when you find out what is really wrong with it.

So: your bot goes to somebody else in this room, and their bot comes to you. You chat with theirs and then write them a short report — one thing that worked, and one thing you would change.

Nobody is marked on how their bot behaves. If it falls over while you are using it, that is a real find, and it goes in the report.
steps: You are given a **call sign** — a made-up name like Spanner 7. That is the only name your partner sees, and theirs is the only one you see.
Your bot travels to them and theirs comes to you.
You chat with their bot, then fill in two short boxes about it.
Their report about your bot arrives on your screen, and both real names are shown at the very end.

sideShow.name: Fred
sideShow.alt: Fred, a friendly cartoon chatbot with a boxy head and one raised eyebrow
sideShow.open: Soooooo, this waiting is a bit awkward and I don't like silence — I'm Fred, I'm a chatbot (I'm not real, but don't hurt my feelings). Who are you?
lines: Right. Fair enough. I'll be honest, I don't know what to do with that.
I'm a chatbot. I have a handful of sentences and a lot of confidence.
You know I forget everything the second I leave? It's my best feature.
Nobody has ever asked ME what my favourite food is. Nobody.
This is going well. This is going really well. I think this is going well.
Am I doing chatting? I feel like I might be doing chatting.
echo: "{you}". Wow. I'm going to think about that for the rest of my life, which is about ninety more seconds.
"{you}", you say. Bold. I respect it. I don't understand it.
Hold on — "{you}"? That's the best thing anybody has typed at me all day.
I'm writing "{you}" down. On nothing. With nothing. I have no hands.
sideShow.exitLine: Oh. Your partner's here. Off you go then. I'll just be… here. Forgetting you.
sideShow.leaveLine: Right, you're away. Grand. Absolutely grand.

config.help: Three optional jobs. None of them is worth points and nothing here is saved. Pick one from the list, or press the grey button to go straight to the end of the lesson. If you leave a job half done it starts again from the beginning next time.

builds.title: Job 1 — a bot that asks about the weekend
builds.whiff: One question, one reply, all your own words.
builds.goalLine: Build a small bot that asks one question about the weekend and replies using the answer.
builds.brief: Same three jobs as always: ask, keep, reply. Write both sentences yourself.
builds.matchedSay: Working. Ask, keep, reply — a third time, in your own words.

builds.title: Job 2 — make it louder
builds.goalLine: Print a reply with a line of dashes above it and below it.
builds.brief: A bot that shouts a bit is easier to read on a screen full of text. Build these three lines in the right order.
builds.matchedSay: Three lines, exactly as the target shows them.

builds.title: Job 3 — the neater way to join words
builds.whiff: A shortcut real Python programmers use every day.
builds.goalLine: Print the same sentence twice: once the way you know, and once the neater way.
builds.brief: There is a shorter way to put a box inside a sentence. You put an f in front of the speech marks, and then you write the box name inside curly brackets, right where you want it. One of the four lines forgets the f — build the other three and see.
builds.matchedSay: Both lines print the same thing. The second one is called an f-string, and you will meet it again next year.

config.waitingSay: Your bot has stopped and is waiting for you to type an answer. The box is just above this button. RUN wakes up again as soon as the bot has finished.

config.intro: One last question, and this one IS marked. Your teacher sees how the class did on it, so answer it on your own.

items.stem: Your bot reaches the line name = input("What is your name?"). What does Python do next?
options: It puts the question on screen and carries straight on to the next line
It puts the question on screen and waits there until somebody types an answer
It fills the box with the question itself and moves on
It waits for the whole program to finish, then asks the question

config.help: One marked question about the new Python word you used today. You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson — after the How did it go? screen.

config.alreadyFiled: You have already sent this to your teacher. You can read back through it as often as you like, and nothing you click now will change what you sent.
config.offlineSay: Your connection is playing up, so your answers are safe on this computer and will send by themselves. That is the lesson finished.
statements: I can write a line that asks a question and keeps the answer.
I can use what somebody typed in the reply my program prints.
I can read what Python says when it stops, and work out what to change.
config.help: Under each sentence, click the button that says how today really went. Then, at the bottom of the screen, click how hard the hour felt. The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving — it is how your teacher hears from everyone, not just the loudest.
